moments.title: Arithmetic and geometric patterns
moments.text: Arithmetic sequences have a common difference; geometric sequences have a common ratio.

moments.title: Term labels
moments.text: $u_1$, $u_2$ and $u_3$ denote the first three terms; $u_n$ denotes term $n$.

moments.title: A negative ratio
moments.text: For $5,-25,125,-625,\ldots$, divide a term by the preceding nonzero term to find $r=-5$.

moments.title: Alternating signs
moments.text: A negative ratio changes the sign at each multiplication when the terms are nonzero.

moments.title: A ratio between zero and one
moments.text: In $100,50,25,12.5,\ldots$, each term is half its predecessor, so $r=1/2$.

moments.title: A negative fractional ratio
moments.text: The sequence $27,-9,3,-1,\ldots$ has $r=-1/3$: signs alternate and magnitudes decrease.

moments.title: Formulas for geometric sequences
moments.text: The presenter identifies the formulas for terms and sums and separates the higher-level infinite-sum formula.

moments.title: Find the eighth term
moments.text: For $u_1=2$ and $r=2$, substitute into $u_n=u_1r^{n-1}$ to obtain $u_8=256$.

moments.title: From terms to a series
moments.text: The next task adds terms rather than finding one term: $S_n$ is the sum of the first $n$ terms.

moments.title: Two equivalent finite-sum formulas
moments.text: For $r\ne1$, $u_1(r^n-1)/(r-1)$ and $u_1(1-r^n)/(1-r)$ give the same sum.

moments.title: An infinite geometric series
moments.text: The video introduces the infinite sum and contrasts shrinking terms with the increasing example.

moments.title: Successive partial sums
moments.text: For a convergent series, adding more terms can bring the partial sum increasingly close to a finite limit; it does not generally become exactly equal to the limit.

notes.title: Condition for an infinite sum
notes.text: The video describes the condition as the common ratio being less than 1. That alone also includes ratios such as $-2$, which do not give a convergent nonzero geometric series.
notes.write: The infinite geometric series converges when $|r|<1$, or equivalently $-1<r<1$. Then $S_\infty=u_1/(1-r)$.

notes.title: Exact limit versus rounded values
notes.text: The presenter says successive partial sums eventually stay the same. They can appear equal after rounding while still changing.
notes.write: For $|r|<1$, the infinite sum is the exact limit of the partial sums; a finite partial sum is generally an approximation to it.

moments.title: Why use sigma notation?
moments.text: Sigma notation is a compact way to write the sum of a sequence of terms.

moments.title: Read the components
moments.text: The sigma indicates addition; the lower and upper limits specify where the index begins and ends.

moments.title: Set up the summand
moments.text: The first example is $\sum_{k=1}^{4}(k+3)$.

moments.title: Substitute each index
moments.text: Use $k=1,2,3,4$ in the expression $k+3$ and add the results.

moments.title: Evaluate the sum
moments.text: The terms are $4,5,6,7$, giving a total of 22.

moments.title: A different starting index
moments.text: The next example starts at $k=3$, not $k=1$, and ends at $k=6$.

moments.title: Write the four terms
moments.text: Substitute $k=3,4,5,6$ into $1/3^k$. Both limits are included.

notes.title: Check the lower limit
notes.text: The first example is written from $k=1$ to $k=4$. The spoken recap is easy to confuse with a different starting value.
notes.write: Use the limits shown in the expression: $\sum_{k=1}^{4}(k+3)=4+5+6+7=22$.

ican.text: I can identify a geometric sequence and calculate its common ratio from consecutive nonzero terms.
I can find a term, first term or ratio using $u_n=u_1r^{n-1}$.
I can find a finite sum and distinguish it from a single term.
I can interpret growth, decay and alternating signs in context.
I can decide whether an infinite geometric series converges and find its sum when it does.

ku.text: A geometric sequence is generated by multiplying each term by the same ratio $r$. For a nonzero term, $r=u_{n+1}/u_n$.
$u_n=u_1r^{n-1}$ because reaching term $n$ from the first term requires $n-1$ multiplications.
If $r<0$ and $u_1\ne0$, successive terms alternate in sign. Their magnitudes decrease when $|r|<1$ and increase when $|r|>1$.
A nonzero geometric series has a finite infinite sum only when $|r|<1$. In that case $S_\infty=u_1/(1-r)$; this is a limit, not the result of adding a finite number of terms.
A sum from $u_a$ to $u_b$ can be found as $S_b-S_{a-1}$; it includes $b-a+1$ terms.

misc.better: Divide successive terms: $r=-25/5=-5$, so the signs alternate.

misc.weak: $r<1$ is enough for an infinite geometric series to converge.
misc.better: Check $|r|<1$. For example $r=-2$ is less than 1 but its nonzero terms do not approach zero.

misc.weak: A formula with denominator $1-r$ works when $r=1$.
misc.better: The denominator is zero at $r=1$. The terms are constant, so $S_n=nu_1$.

misc.weak: The sum from term 4 to term 10 is $S_{10}-S_4$.

terms.text: Divide a term by the previous nonzero term and check the ratio is consistent.
Identify the first term and the number of terms, then use an applicable finite-sum expression.
Test the magnitude of the ratio before applying the infinite-sum formula.

worked.prompt: A ball is dropped from a height of $2$ m. Each rebound reaches $60\%$ of the previous height. Let $u_n$ be the height of rebound $n$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.a: The first rebound reaches $u_1=2(0.6)=1.2$ m and $r=0.6$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Find the height of the fourth rebound.
parts.a: $u_4=1.2(0.6)^3=0.2592$ m, or $0.259$ m to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Find the sum of the heights of the first four rebounds.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Find the infinite sum of the rebound heights. Explain what this sum represents.
parts.a: Since $|0.6|<1$, $S_\infty=1.2/(1-0.6)=3$ m. This adds the maximum heights reached on rebound; it is not the total distance travelled.

kq.model: $u_1$ is already the first term. Reaching term $n$ takes $n-1$ multiplications by $r$.

kq.q: Why does $r=-2$ fail the infinite-sum test even though $-2<1$?
kq.model: Its magnitude is 2. Unless the first term is zero, the magnitudes of the terms grow and do not approach zero.

kq.q: Why is an infinite sum not usually equal to a finite partial sum?
kq.model: The infinite sum is the limit as the number of terms grows. For a nonzero geometric sequence with $0<|r|<1$, a finite remainder generally remains.

kq.q: Why is the sum of rebound heights not the ball's total distance?
kq.model: It counts the upward rebound heights once each. Total distance also includes the initial fall and the subsequent downward journeys.
